episodes.title: Week 0–1: Hello, World
episodes.subtitle: Birth to day 7
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to your very first week together. Grab a glass of water, sit back, and let's talk about what's normal right now, from the first hours through day seven.

Let's start with diapers, because they are your best clue that feeding is going well. In the first day or two, expect just one or two wet diapers a day, and those first poops are sticky, dark, almost tar-like. That's meconium, and it's completely normal. Each day the count climbs, and by around day five or six you'll want to see about six or more wet diapers a day. The poop changes too, from dark green to a mustardy yellow if your baby is breastfed.

Now, feeding. A newborn's tummy is tiny, so feeds are small and frequent. Breastfed babies usually eat eight to twelve times in twenty-four hours, roughly every two to three hours, day and night. If you're using formula, many newborns take about one to two ounces per feed in the first days, every two to three hours. Follow hunger cues, like rooting and hands to the mouth, more than the clock. And check with your pediatrician about how feeding is going, especially weight.

What can your baby see? Things about eight to twelve inches away, which happens to be just about the distance to your face during a feed. Bold, high-contrast shapes, like black and white, are easiest to see.

Sleep comes in short stretches, adding up to around sixteen hours a day. Every single time, remember the ABCs: Alone, on their Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface, and nothing else in it. Your pediatrician can help with any sleep questions.

Here's a fun fact: newborns already prefer looking at faces over almost anything else. You are their favorite show.

Coming up: around two to three weeks, many babies hit a growth spurt and want to cluster feed, eating again and again in a short window. It's normal, and it passes.

One last thing. Fever, trouble breathing, too few wet diapers, or yellow skin are reasons to call your pediatrician right away. You're doing great. See you next week.

episodes.title: Week 1: Finding Your Rhythm
episodes.subtitle: Days 7–14
episodes.transcript:
Your baby is one week old. You made it through the first seven days, and that's a big deal. Let's talk about what week two, days seven to fourteen, usually looks like.

First, diapers. By now, expect about six or more wet diapers a day, with pale yellow pee. Breastfed babies often have several soft, seedy, mustard-yellow poops a day at this age, sometimes after nearly every feed. Formula-fed babies tend to have fewer, firmer ones, more tan or yellow. Lots of variation is normal, so keep a rough tally and bring it to your next checkup.

Feeding is still frequent. Breastfed babies usually nurse eight to twelve times a day. Formula-fed babies often take about two to three ounces per feed, every three to four hours. One big milestone this week: most babies are back to their birth weight by around ten to fourteen days old. Your pediatrician will track that, so check with them about how feeding is going.

Your baby's world is still close up. They see best about eight to twelve inches away, and they love bold, high-contrast patterns and your face. Try a little supervised tummy time while they're awake, just a few minutes at a time. It builds neck and shoulder strength.

Sleep is still around sixteen hours a day, in short stretches. Keep up the ABCs: Alone, on their Back, in a Crib or bassinet. Room sharing, without bed sharing, is recommended. Any sleep worries, ask your pediatrician.

Something else this week: the umbilical cord stump usually falls off somewhere between one and three weeks. Keep it clean and dry, and call if you notice redness, swelling, or a bad smell.

Fun fact: put your finger in your baby's palm and watch them grip it. That's the grasp reflex, and it's surprisingly strong.

Heads-up for what's next: the two-to-three-week growth spurt. Expect cluster feeding, fussier evenings, and a baby who seems hungry all the time. It's temporary. Feed on demand, rest when you can, and tag-team with each other.

And as always, fever in a baby this young is a reason to call your pediatrician right away. See you next week.

episodes.title: Week 2: The First Growth Spurt
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week two, days fourteen through twenty-one: the first growth spurt, and finding your feet. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This week at a glance.

By day fourteen, most healthy term babies are back to birth weight. The AAP expects that by about ten to fourteen days. From here, many babies gain roughly two thirds of an ounce to an ounce a day in the early months, but your pediatrician reads the growth curve over time, not one weigh-in.

Many families notice a growth spurt somewhere around two to three weeks. It often looks like a baby who suddenly wants to feed again and again, especially in the evening, and seems hard to settle. It usually passes in a few days, and it isn't, by itself, proof that milk is running out.

Crying also tends to climb from about two weeks and peak around six to eight weeks. A baby who cries more this week is usually doing something normal.

The umbilical stump usually falls off by about three weeks. Keep it clean and dry, and call for spreading redness, pus, or a foul smell.

Chapter two. Senses and the growing brain.

Vision at this age is blurry. Babies see best at about eight to twelve inches, roughly the distance to your face during a feed. They prefer high contrast and faces. Color vision develops over the first few months and is fairly good by about four to five months, so bold patterns beat pastels for now. It is also common for the eyes to drift or cross briefly. That is expected in the early months, but eyes that stay crossed or turned past about four months deserve a check.

Hearing is working, and familiar voices draw attention. The best brain exercise is what Harvard's Center on the Developing Child calls serve and return: baby makes a face, sound, or look, and you answer it. Narrate, sing, and hold eye contact in quiet alert moments. The CDC recommends no screen time before age two, other than video calls with family.

The natural lens. Montessori families often hang a black-and-white Munari mobile above a floor mat, and Magda Gerber's RIE approach favors calm attention and unhurried floor time over gadgets. Evidence for any particular mobile is thin, but the reasoning holds: contrast suits young eyes, and a calm face is the richest stimulus a newborn has.

Chapter three. Movement and tummy time.

Movements are mostly reflexes right now: startle, grasp, and stepping when held upright. They fade over the coming months.

Tummy time starts now. The AAP's 2022 safe sleep report says to begin supervised tummy time soon after coming home, and to build toward fifteen to thirty minutes total per day by about seven weeks. This week, think two or three sessions of a few minutes each, after a diaper change, while baby is awake and you are right there. Lying tummy-to-chest on a reclined parent counts as a gentle start.

The natural lens. Natural-movement advocates favor floor time over car seats, swings, and bouncers, and the AAP agrees that limiting time in carriers and bouncers helps prevent flat spots. If you babywear, keep the face visible, chin off the chest, and baby close enough to kiss.

Chapter four. Feeding, four ways.

We break feeding into four routes, because a number from one route should never quietly become the benchmark for another.

Feeding at the breast. The CDC and AAP describe eight to twelve feeds in twenty-four hours in the early weeks, and cluster feeding during a growth spurt is common. A nursing timer measures minutes, not milk. The signs of enough are steady weight gain, six or more wet diapers a day, and regular yellow stools. For context only, the Neville study from Denver in 1988 weighed directly nursed, exclusively breastfed babies before and after every feed. At day fourteen, the average was about six hundred thirty-four milliliters, or twenty-one ounces, in twenty-four hours, but individual babies ranged from about four hundred to nearly nine hundred milliliters. At day twenty-one, the average was similar. That was thirteen families: context, not a target.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. You have a measured number here, but no validated bottle-specific requirement for a two-week-old. Two to three ounces per bottle is a common early range borrowed from formula guidance, so treat it as a loose starting point and follow cues. Many lactation professionals recommend paced bottle feeding: baby fairly upright, bottle closer to horizontal, with pauses, so the flow feels more like the breast. That is professional practice more than trial evidence. If you're pumping, the Little Steps Pumps tab compares logged totals with an exclusive-pumping study and a separate full-supply reference. For storage, the CDC says freshly expressed milk is fine for up to four hours at room temperature and up to four days in the fridge.

Formula. AAP guidance is about two to three ounces per feed in these weeks, moving toward three to four ounces every three to four hours by the end of the first month. A rough planning guide is about two and a half ounces per pound of body weight per day, usually not more than about thirty-two ounces. Don't push a baby to finish.

Mixed feeding. Count bottle ounces as measured, and count breast feeds as feeds. Do not add a guessed number for the breast. If a bottle replaces a breast feed and you want to protect supply, lactation guidance is to pump around that time. In a 2016 study by Kent and colleagues, breastfeeding mothers who also pumped expressed a median of about a hundred sixty-eight milliliters a day, so pumped totals are only part of production.

The natural lens on formula. The FDA's Operation Stork Speed, part of the Make America Healthy Again effort, is reviewing formula nutrients for the first time since 1998, and its October twenty-ninth, 2026 testing update found most samples had low or non-detectable heavy metals. Many families in this movement prefer organic or whole-milk-fat formulas; all legal U.S. formula meets the same FDA nutrient standards, and the FDA warns against homemade or raw milk formula. On plastics, the AAP and natural voices agree: don't microwave milk or formula or heat it in plastic. Glass or stainless bottles are a reasonable choice.

Vitamin D. The AAP recommends four hundred international units a day for babies who get any breast milk, starting in the first days. The natural lens: a 2015 randomized trial by Hollis and Wagner, published in Pediatrics, found that mothers taking sixty-four hundred units a day supplied enough vitamin D through breast milk that their babies matched infants given drops. That trial started at four to six weeks postpartum. It's a real alternative to discuss with your pediatrician, not something to switch to on your own.

The parent's plate. A nursing mother needs roughly three hundred thirty to four hundred extra calories a day, according to the CDC. The new 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines put eating real food at the center, with protein at every meal and full-fat dairy, and that overlaps with what dietitian Lily Nichols, author of Real Food for Pregnancy, teaches about eggs, meat, fish, and nourishing whole foods after birth. If you eat low-carb, keto, or carnivore, there is one caution worth knowing. Case reports describe lactation ketoacidosis, a rare but serious condition, in breastfeeding women on very low-carb diets, especially with fasting or under-eating. Our reasoning: in these early weeks, eat enough, drink to thirst, don't fast, and talk with your clinician before going strictly ketogenic.

Chapter five. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Newborns sleep a lot, often sixteen hours or more, in short stretches day and night. Every sleep follows the ABCs: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet with a firm, flat surface and nothing else in it. The AAP recommends sharing your room, not your bed, ideally for at least the first six months.

The natural lens. Light sets the body clock. A 2004 study by Yvonne Harrison followed fifty-six babies at six, nine, and twelve weeks and found that babies who slept better at night were exposed to more light in the early afternoon. That's a link, not proof, but the reasoning is low-risk: bright days, dim nights. Feed by a window or sit outside in the shade by day, and keep night feeds dark and quiet. The AAP advises keeping babies under six months out of direct sun, so shade and window light are your tools for now. And sunlight is not a home treatment for jaundice.

Chapter six. Looking ahead.

Not on the agenda yet, but coming: the first social smile, usually around six to eight weeks. Teething, most often around six months, with a wide range. Rolling tummy to back, on the CDC's six-month list. Sitting alone, between about four and nine months in the WHO motor study, and walking alone, between about eight and eighteen months. Solid foods start around six months with signs of readiness. Until then, breast milk or formula is the whole menu: no water, no cereal in bottles.

Chapter seven. What this means, and what to do.

First, expect more feeding and fussing, and think growth spurt before anything else. Weight checks and diapers are your truth, not the clock.

Second, start tummy time: two or three short sessions a day, awake and watched.

Third, give the day bright light and the night darkness.

Fourth, log by route: bottles in ounces, breast feeds as feeds, pumping in the Pumps tab.

Fifth, eat real food and plenty of it, and don't fast while you're nursing.

Sixth, check on the parents. Baby blues usually ease within about two weeks of birth. Sadness or anxiety that lasts longer, or feels heavy, deserves a call to your own clinician. Help works.

When to call. If your baby is three months or younger and has a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, or higher, call your pediatrician right away. Call too for fewer wet diapers, poor feeding, trouble breathing, unusual sleepiness, green vomit, pale or white stools, or yellow skin that's spreading or still there past two weeks. In an emergency, call nine one one.

Sources and method. The baseline comes from AAP HealthyChildren pages and its 2022 safe sleep report, the CDC, the NHS, the WHO, and the named studies: Neville 1988, Kent 2016, Hollis and Wagner 2015, and Harrison 2004. Natural-lens material names its source and is opinion or emerging evidence unless we said otherwise. Links are in the Sources tab. This is general education, not a replacement for your baby's clinician. See you in week three.

episodes.title: Week 3: More Awake, More Opinionated
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week three, days twenty-one through twenty-eight: more awake, more opinionated. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

How this works: each chapter starts with the mainstream baseline, from the American Academy of Pediatrics, the CDC, the World Health Organization, and named studies. Then comes the natural lens, from functional medicine, whole-food, and Make America Healthy Again voices. Where evidence is thin, we'll call our thinking reasoning, not fact. Study numbers describe the babies studied, not targets for yours.

Chapter one. This week at a glance.

Week three often brings longer stretches of quiet alertness: eyes open, scanning, calm. It also often brings a fussier evening. Many babies have a late-afternoon or evening window of crying and cluster feeding, and the overall crying curve is still rising toward its usual peak around six to eight weeks. That is normal development, not a sign you are doing something wrong.

Weight gain should be steady now that birth weight is regained, roughly two thirds of an ounce to an ounce a day for many babies. The one-month checkup is coming up. It's a good time to start a short list of questions.

Spit-up is very common. Most babies who spit up are what pediatricians call happy spitters: growing well, comfortable, and just messy. Small, effortless spit-ups after feeds are expected.

Chapter two. Senses and the growing brain.

Your baby's focus is still best at about eight to twelve inches, but you may notice longer gazes and brief tracking of a slowly moving face. High-contrast patterns and the human face remain the favorite things to look at. Color vision is developing and is fairly good by about four to five months.

Brain exercise for this week: copy your baby. When they open their mouth, open yours. When they make a sound, make it back. This is serve and return, the back-and-forth that Harvard's Center on the Developing Child describes as building the architecture of the brain. Read aloud, even adult books. What matters is your voice and rhythm. The CDC recommends no screen time before age two, except video calls.

The natural lens. Functional and natural-parenting voices emphasize skin-to-skin contact beyond the hospital days, for regulation, bonding, and breastfeeding. The mainstream evidence for skin-to-skin is strongest right after birth, but there's no downside to continuing it when you're awake and alert. Our reasoning: it costs nothing, and it's what your baby is built for.

Chapter three. Movement and tummy time.

Reflexes still lead the way. You may see a little more head lifting during tummy time, usually just for a moment and wobbly. That's the point: tummy time is strength training.

Keep building toward the AAP target of fifteen to thirty minutes total per day by about seven weeks. A practical week-three goal is three or four short sessions a day, a few minutes each, on a firm surface, awake and watched. If your baby protests, try a rolled towel under the chest, get down face to face, or do tummy-to-chest on a reclined parent.

The natural lens. Natural-movement advocates suggest a firm floor mat over bouncers and swings, and the AAP agrees that too much time in carriers and seats raises the risk of flat spots. Free floor time is a low-cost, low-risk habit, and the earlier it starts, the easier it is.

Chapter four. Feeding, four ways.

As always, four routes, kept separate.

Feeding at the breast. Eight to twelve feeds in twenty-four hours is still the typical range, with cluster feeding in the evening. For context only, the Neville study from Denver in 1988, which weighed directly nursed, exclusively breastfed babies before and after every feed, found an average of about six hundred thirty milliliters, around twenty-one ounces, per day at day twenty-one, and about seven hundred fifty milliliters, around twenty-five ounces, at day twenty-eight. The range at day twenty-eight ran from under five hundred to over eleven hundred milliliters. That's thirteen families, so read it as context, not a goal. Your proof is weight and diapers.

Pumped breast milk in a bottle. If you plan to use bottles, many lactation professionals suggest introducing one once breastfeeding is going well, often around three to four weeks. That's practical guidance, not a firm rule. There is still no validated bottle-specific requirement for this age. Many babies take roughly two to four ounces per bottle around now, but that range is borrowed from formula guidance, so follow cues. Use paced bottle feeding, and keep up the CDC storage rules: up to four hours at room temperature and four days in the fridge for fresh milk. The Little Steps Pumps tab shows logged pumping totals against an exclusive-pumping study and a separate full-supply reference, and it notes that the study ends at day fourteen.

Formula. AAP guidance moves toward about three to four ounces every three to four hours by the end of the first month. A rough guide is two and a half ounces per pound per day, usually capped around thirty-two ounces. Follow fullness cues: turning away, slowing down, relaxed hands.

Mixed feeding. Log bottle ounces as measured, and breast feeds as feeds. Don't add guessed ounces for the breast. If bottles are replacing nursing sessions and you want to keep your supply, pumping around those times helps signal your body to keep making milk.

Pacifiers. The AAP says offering a pacifier at sleep time is linked to a lower risk of SIDS, and for breastfed babies, to wait until breastfeeding is well established, often around three to four weeks. Never force it, and don't put it back in if it falls out during sleep.

The natural lens on spit-up. Integrative pediatrician Dr. Elisa Song, author of Healthy Kids, Happy Kids, argues against reaching quickly for acid-suppressing medicine for an infant's spit-up because of its possible effects on the gut microbiome. Mainstream pediatric gastroenterology guidance actually agrees: acid suppression isn't recommended for uncomplicated spit-up in a thriving baby. Shared first steps are smaller, more frequent feeds, burping, and keeping baby upright after feeds while awake.

The parent's plate. The new 2025 to 2030 Dietary Guidelines put eating real food at the center, with protein at each meal and full-fat dairy. Real-food dietitian Lily Nichols emphasizes nutrient-dense staples like eggs for choline, fatty fish for omega-3s, and meat for iron and B12. If you eat low-carb or carnivore, keep calories up and don't fast. Lactation ketoacidosis is rare, but case reports tie it to very low-carb diets and under-eating while breastfeeding. Our reasoning is that a moderate approach is safer than a strict ketogenic one in these early weeks; talk with your clinician before going strict.

Chapter five. Sleep, light, and rhythm.

Sleep is still scattered across day and night, often sixteen hours or more in total. The ABCs every time: Alone, on the Back, in a Crib or bassinet on a firm, flat surface with nothing else in it. Room-share, don't bed-share, ideally for the first six months. Swaddling is fine if baby is placed on the back, the hips can move freely, and you stop once baby shows signs of trying to roll.

The natural lens. Babies aren't born with a working day-night rhythm; it develops over the first months. In Yvonne Harrison's 2004 study of babies at six to twelve weeks, better night sleepers got more early-afternoon light. That's a link, not proof, but the reasoning is low-risk: daytime naps in a bright room, a walk in the shade, and dark, quiet, boring night feeds. Keep babies under six months out of direct sun.

Chapter six. Looking ahead.

Coming soon: the first true social smile, usually around six to eight weeks; the CDC lists smiling when you talk on its two-month checklist. Cooing follows. Not yet: teething, most often around six months with a wide range; rolling, on the CDC's six-month list; sitting alone, between about four and nine months in the WHO motor study; and walking alone, between about eight and eighteen months. Solid foods start around six months with readiness signs. Until then, only breast milk or formula: no water, no cereal in bottles.

Chapter seven. What this means, and what to do.

First, plan for the evening fussy window. Line up help, dim the lights, and have a calming routine ready: feed, rock, sway, shush.

Second, keep tummy time growing: three or four short sessions a day.

Third, if bottles are part of your plan, this is a reasonable window to try one, with paced feeding.

Fourth, if spit-up isn't bothering your baby and weight is good, it's usually laundry, not illness.

Fifth, protect the day-night signal: bright days, dark nights.

Sixth, write down your questions for the one-month visit, including how you, the parents, are doing.

When to call. If your baby is three months or younger and has a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, or higher, call your pediatrician right away. Call too for forceful or projectile vomiting, green vomit, blood in spit-up or stool, poor weight gain, fewer wet diapers, trouble breathing, unusual sleepiness, or crying that seems like pain and won't settle. If you ever feel overwhelmed, put the baby down safely in the crib and step away for a few minutes. Never shake a baby. In an emergency, call nine one one.

Sources and method. The baseline comes from AAP HealthyChildren pages and its 2022 safe sleep report, the CDC, the WHO, and the named studies: Neville 1988 and Harrison 2004. Natural-lens material names its source and is opinion or emerging evidence unless we said otherwise. Links are in the Sources tab. This is general education, not a replacement for your baby's clinician. See you in week four.

episodes.title: Week 4
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week four: Small moments of play. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

You do not need a shelf full of toys to make this week interesting. Your face, your voice, and a few minutes together are plenty. When your baby is awake and comfortable, get close, talk gently, and pause. Notice whether they look toward you or seem ready for a break. Turning away or fussing is a cue to slow down, not to try harder.

Try a little supervised tummy time while the baby is awake. Stay right there, start briefly, and build up gradually as tolerated. The American Academy of Pediatrics suggests working toward a total of fifteen to thirty minutes a day by seven weeks. That is a gradual goal across short sessions, not a demand for one long workout. If this is difficult or there are medical concerns, ask for help adapting it.

Play on the tummy; sleep on the back. If the baby gets sleepy, move to the proper safe sleep space. Today's activity is one short, comfortable play session, stopped before it becomes a battle.

One safety reminder: at three months or younger, a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, needs an immediate call to the pediatrician. This is general guidance, not a replacement for your baby's care plan. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.subtitle: Days 28–35

episodes.title: Week 5
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week five: Protect the sleep space. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

Think of bedtime as a safety reset, even if bedtime happens six times today. Before each sleep, check the space: a firm, flat mattress in a safety-approved crib or bassinet, a fitted sheet, and nothing loose. Put your baby down on their back. Pillows, blankets, positioners, and weighted sleep products do not belong there.

If your baby falls asleep in a swing, stroller, or car seat, move them to a firm, flat sleep surface as soon as possible. A car seat is for safe travel, not a replacement crib at home. Keep the baby's sleep space in your room, but not in your bed; the AAP recommends room sharing for at least the first six months.

The hardest moment may be the feed when you are exhausted. Plan a caregiver handoff before you are nodding off, and avoid falling asleep with the baby on a sofa or armchair. Tonight's practical win is a clear sleep space and a realistic plan for the tired adult.

One safety reminder: at three months or younger, a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, needs an immediate call to the pediatrician. This is general guidance, not a replacement for your baby's care plan. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.subtitle: Days 35–42

episodes.title: Week 6
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week six: Your first conversations. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

A conversation can start long before words. During a calm awake moment, look at your baby and say something simple, then wait. If there is a sound, a movement, or a look back, respond warmly. You are practicing taking turns, not testing performance.

The CDC's two-month checklist includes looking at faces, making sounds other than crying, and smiling when spoken to or smiled at. Those are reference points for the coming weeks, not a prediction that a particular skill must appear today. The checklists describe skills most children can do by the listed age; they do not diagnose a child.

Keep the activity easy. Read a few lines, sing a familiar song, or describe the clean diaper you are putting on. If your baby looks away, yawns, or becomes fussy, offer a break. Your voice matters more than finishing the page. Today's little assignment: find one quiet moment for a back-and-forth exchange, and enjoy whatever response you get.

One safety reminder: at three months or younger, a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, needs an immediate call to the pediatrician. This is general guidance, not a replacement for your baby's care plan. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.subtitle: Days 42–49

episodes.title: Week 7
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week seven: Move a little, rest a little. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

Imagine the floor as a tiny practice studio. A safe play surface, an awake baby, and an attentive adult are the essentials. Short tummy-time sessions give opportunities to work on lifting the head and looking around. The AAP's gradual goal by this age is fifteen to thirty minutes total across the day, adjusted to what your baby can tolerate.

Put your face or an age-appropriate toy at eye level and stay beside the baby. You are offering an invitation, not pushing through distress. If movement seems uncomfortable or one-sided, bring that observation to the clinician. A short video of what worries you can help explain the concern.

Keep sleep separate from exercise. Always start sleep on the back in an empty, firm, flat sleep space. If you swaddle, stop as soon as there are signs of trying to roll; do not wait for a certain birthday. This week's win is gentle practice with plenty of breaks, not hitting a personal record.

One safety reminder: at three months or younger, a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, needs an immediate call to the pediatrician. This is general guidance, not a replacement for your baby's care plan. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.subtitle: Days 49–56

episodes.title: Week 8
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week eight: Make the checkup useful. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

The two-month visit can feel like a lot to remember. Make it easier before you arrive: choose a few questions about feeding, growth, sleep, or development. Bring the feeding log as context, not as a report card. A clinician can interpret it alongside the baby's growth and examination.

The CDC's two-month checklist includes looking at your face, reacting to loud sounds, moving both arms and legs, and holding the head up during tummy time. Notice what you see, and mention anything that concerns you. If a skill has been lost, do not wait for the next routine visit to speak up.

Ask the care team which immunizations are due and what to expect afterward. Also ask about vitamin D: breastfed babies and babies drinking less than about thirty-two ounces of formula daily generally need a supplement. Have the clinician confirm the product and dose rather than guessing from a dropper. Your practical task today is a short question list. The appointment is a partnership, not an exam you need to pass.

One safety reminder: at three months or younger, a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, needs an immediate call to the pediatrician. This is general guidance, not a replacement for your baby's care plan. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.subtitle: Days 56–63
episodes.feeding_route_note: Here “breastfed” in the vitamin D discussion includes babies receiving human milk directly at the breast or expressed in a bottle. It refers to milk type, not a route-specific intake benchmark; confirm the supplement plan with the clinician.

episodes.title: Week 9
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week nine: Less stimulation, more connection. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

Sometimes the best baby activity is doing less. If you have a few awake minutes, try one simple thing: a face, a song, or a safe toy to watch. Then pause and see whether your baby wants more. Looking away or becoming fussy can mean it is time for a break.

The next developmental reference point is the CDC's four-month checklist. It includes cooing, turning toward a familiar voice, and bringing hands to the mouth. Those are skills to watch for over the coming weeks, not requirements for week nine. Avoid comparing today's performance with a video of somebody else's baby.

For play, put away your own screen when possible and narrate the ordinary things you are doing. Babies learn through people responding to them; they do not need a learning video. Keep offering supervised floor time during waking hours, and use the proper safe space for every sleep. This week's takeaway: a few responsive moments are more useful than a packed activity schedule.

One safety reminder: at three months or younger, a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, needs an immediate call to the pediatrician. This is general guidance, not a replacement for your baby's care plan. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.subtitle: Days 63–70

episodes.title: Week 10
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week ten: Feeding without a contest. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

Here is a common trap: the bottle still has milk in it, so it feels unfinished. But a baby closing their mouth or turning away may be telling you they are full. Notice hunger cues and fullness cues rather than treating the container as the goal.

Feeds vary in length and spacing, and direct nursing cannot be converted into ounces just by timing it. With mixed feeding, bottle volume is only the measured part of intake. If the log raises a worry, pair that information with a conversation about growth and feeding effectiveness instead of automatically adding a bigger feed.

This is still the milk-feeding stage: breast milk or infant formula, not early solids or water to stretch between feeds. Ask the clinician if there is any concern about intake or growth. Today's practical action is to watch one feed without multitasking. Notice how hunger starts, how swallowing sounds, and how the baby signals they are done. Those observations can be useful at your next visit.

One safety reminder: at three months or younger, a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, needs an immediate call to the pediatrician. This is general guidance, not a replacement for your baby's care plan. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.subtitle: Days 70–77
episodes.feeding_route_note: Mixed feeding can mean direct nursing plus bottles, or formula and expressed breast milk in bottles. Bottle totals omit milk transferred during any direct nursing; a complete bottle-only record can measure total taken from bottles. A bottle containing both milks is different from a mixed feeding regimen.

episodes.title: Week 11
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week eleven: Before the first roll. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

A new movement can arrive without much warning. Prepare now rather than waiting until a roll has already happened. If your baby shows signs of trying to roll, stop swaddling immediately. Use suitable non-weighted sleep clothing instead. The trigger is the baby's movement, not a calendar date.

Always start sleep on the back. Later, when a baby can comfortably roll both ways, the AAP says you do not need to keep turning them back, but the sleep space must remain empty. Do not use wedges, pillows, or positioners to hold a baby still.

During awake time, keep play on a safe floor surface with supervision. The four-month reference points ahead include holding the head steady when held and pushing onto forearms during tummy time. There is no need to force those skills today. Your practical task is a quick review of every sleep space and a chat with every caregiver about stopping swaddling at the first signs of rolling.

One safety reminder: at three months or younger, a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, needs an immediate call to the pediatrician. This is general guidance, not a replacement for your baby's care plan. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.subtitle: Days 77–84

episodes.title: Week 12
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Week twelve: A bridge, not a deadline. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

The weekly chapter is ending, and the monthly chapter is about to begin. There is no magical switch at twelve weeks. Feeding, sleep, and development still change in uneven little steps. This episode is a chance to notice patterns without demanding a perfect routine.

Look ahead to the four-month CDC checklist: cooing, responding with sounds, holding a toy placed in the hand, and bringing hands to the mouth are useful examples. Offer opportunities through talking and supervised play. Do not drill, and do not wait to ask for help if you are concerned or a skill disappears.

Continue breast milk or formula, respond to feeding cues, and use the safe sleep setup every time. A calm sequence before sleep can be simple: feed as needed, a quiet voice, then the crib. A routine is a familiar order of events, not a guarantee of sleeping through the night. Your task this week is to keep what helps and drop one unnecessary pressure. Next, the library follows development month by month.

One safety reminder: at three months or younger, a rectal temperature of one hundred point four degrees Fahrenheit, or thirty-eight Celsius, needs an immediate call to the pediatrician. This is general guidance, not a replacement for your baby's care plan. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.subtitle: Days 84–91

episodes.title: Month 3
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month three: Build a flexible rhythm. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

Picture a day with a little more predictability, but plenty of surprises. Rather than setting a rigid timetable, try repeating a few gentle cues: conversation during a diaper change, a short play session when alert, and quieter surroundings before sleep. Keep feeding responsive to hunger and fullness.

Your baby's next CDC milestone checkpoint is four months. You may start watching for interest in hands, cooing, or attempts to keep your attention. These are possibilities to notice, not claims about what your baby is doing already. Respond to sounds, offer a safe easy-to-hold toy, and give supervised floor time.

Rolling preparation matters now. Stop swaddling at any sign of trying to roll, and always start sleep on the back. Breast milk or formula remains the food at this stage; being curious about your dinner does not by itself mean readiness for solids. Today's useful goal is one dependable calming routine and one enjoyable face-to-face moment. If development or feeding worries you, bring it up rather than waiting for an app to tell you everything is fine.

These are general ideas, not a substitute for your child's care plan. If feeding, growth, or development worries you, ask your clinician. Sources are included with this episode. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.subtitle: 3 months

episodes.title: Month 4
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month four: Hands become an adventure. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

Watch those hands. The CDC's four-month checklist includes looking at hands with interest, bringing them to the mouth, and holding a toy placed in the hand. Offer a clean, age-appropriate toy that is not sharp, hot, or small enough to choke on. Stay involved and let the baby explore at their own pace.

Talk back when your baby makes sounds. Read a picture book by naming what you see, even if you only make it through one page. During supervised tummy time, give space to push up and look around. If a milestone is missing or you have concerns, discuss it with the clinician; the checklist is a conversation starter, not a diagnosis.

This is also a good time to plan for solids, not rush them. General guidance is around six months when the baby is developmentally ready, and not before four months. Until then, breast milk or formula continues. Keep the sleep space empty, and stop swaddling with any rolling attempts. Today's job is one safe toy and a few minutes of shared exploration.

These are general ideas, not a substitute for your child's care plan. If feeding, growth, or development worries you, ask your clinician. Sources are included with this episode. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.subtitle: 4 months

episodes.title: Month 5
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month five: Get ready, without rushing. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

The family table may suddenly look fascinating. Watching you eat is a lovely social moment, but interest alone is not the green light for solids. Around six months, look for a collection of readiness signs: steady head and neck control, sitting with support or alone, opening the mouth for food, and swallowing rather than pushing everything back out.

Use this month to talk with your clinician about first foods and choking prevention. If your baby has severe eczema or an egg allergy, ask specifically about safely introducing peanut-containing foods. There is no need to buy an elaborate feeding system to have this conversation.

For now, offer responsive milk feeds and supervised floor play. The next CDC checkpoint, at six months, includes reaching for a wanted toy, laughing, and taking turns making sounds. You can support those opportunities without making them homework. Put a safe toy nearby, respond to a squeal, and pause. Today's action is preparation: write down your questions about readiness and choose a calm, supervised place for future meals.

These are general ideas, not a substitute for your child's care plan. If feeding, growth, or development worries you, ask your clinician. Sources are included with this episode. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.subtitle: 5 months

episodes.title: Month 6
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month six: First tastes, safely. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

Imagine a small spoonful, a puzzled expression, and most of it landing on the bib. Starting solids is practice, not a race to replace milk. Around six months, when readiness signs are present, begin developmentally suitable foods while continuing breast milk or formula as the main source of nutrition.

Start with a small amount of a single-ingredient food. The CDC advises waiting three to five days between new foods initially so problems are easier to spot. Offer variety over time, including fortified infant cereal and other foods from different groups. Keep textures soft and appropriate, and stay right beside your baby for eating.

Potential allergens belong in the introduction plan, not on an automatic delay list. Ask first about peanut introduction if there is severe eczema or egg allergy. Whole nuts and spoonfuls of thick nut butter are not safe serving forms. No honey before twelve months, and no cow's milk as the main drink before then. Today's goal is a safe, calm first experience, not a clean bowl.

These are general ideas, not a substitute for your child's care plan. If feeding, growth, or development worries you, ask your clinician. Sources are included with this episode. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.subtitle: 6 months

episodes.title: Month 7
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month seven: Let the menu grow. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

The menu can begin to feel more like a tiny version of family food. By seven or eight months, many babies can explore foods from several food groups, prepared safely for their skills. Think soft vegetables, fruit, proteins, and a variety of fortified cereals, not one food expected to do every job.

Texture changes should follow ability, with you watching closely. Mash or puree food as needed, cook hard foods until soft, and remove bones, pits, and other hazards. Never hand over a whole grape or a round slice of sausage. Eating happens seated and supervised, not while wandering or riding around.

Watch for fullness: closing the mouth or turning away is information, not a challenge to overcome. Continue breast milk or formula, and let the clinician guide you if intake or growth is concerning. Your small task today is to offer one safe texture or flavor without pressure. A funny face does not prove a permanent dislike. You can offer the food again another day while keeping the experience calm.

These are general ideas, not a substitute for your child's care plan. If feeding, growth, or development worries you, ask your clinician. Sources are included with this episode. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.subtitle: 7 months

episodes.title: Month 8
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month eight: A safe place to explore. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

Get down to floor level for a moment and look around. What can little hands reach? As movement changes, a room that was safe last month may need another review. Move sharp and breakable things, lock away medicines and cleaning products, and remove small objects from the play area.

Offer a safe toy a little out of reach and stay close while the baby works out how to approach it. There is no need to force crawling or compare one movement style with another. The nine-month CDC checklist ahead includes sitting without support, getting into sitting, and transferring things between hands. Ask about any concerns rather than turning one skill into the whole story.

Play can be delightfully ordinary: pass a toy back and forth, name a picture, or repeat a sound. Keep meals seated and supervised, with food prepared for the baby's current skills. Today's action is a floor-level safety sweep, then a few minutes of play together. Safe space plus your attention is more valuable than a complicated activity.

These are general ideas, not a substitute for your child's care plan. If feeding, growth, or development worries you, ask your clinician. Sources are included with this episode. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.subtitle: 8 months

episodes.title: Month 9
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month nine: The disappearing spoon game. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

The spoon drops. You pick it up. It drops again. This may feel repetitive, but looking for dropped objects is one of the skills on the CDC's nine-month checklist. A simple back-and-forth game gives you a way to share the discovery without needing a new toy.

At this checkpoint, notice sitting without support, varied babbling, looking when called by name, and moving objects between hands. These checklists describe what most babies can do by an age, and they are not diagnostic tests. Share concerns or lost skills with your clinician promptly, and ask about developmental screening.

Some babies also react more strongly when a caregiver leaves. Try a short, cheerful goodbye rather than sneaking away, and greet them warmly when you return. Keep familiar routines and allow time to get used to another caregiver. Today's practical plan is one little turn-taking game and one predictable goodbye. Your baby does not need to handle every new situation happily for you to be supporting them well.

These are general ideas, not a substitute for your child's care plan. If feeding, growth, or development worries you, ask your clinician. Sources are included with this episode. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.subtitle: 9 months

episodes.title: Month 10
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month ten: Small hands, big experiments. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

A cup, a safe container, and a few large baby-safe toys can turn the floor into a discovery lab. Show putting a toy in and taking it out. Let your baby watch or join in, without requiring a particular result. The one-year CDC checkpoint ahead includes putting something into a container and finding a toy hidden in front of them.

Keep talking through everyday moments. Name the cup, describe the ball, and respond to sounds or gestures. A shared picture book can be a conversation about pictures rather than a full reading of the words. Real back-and-forth matters more than a learning video.

At meals, continue safe textures and close supervision. Small foods must be prepared to avoid choking; small does not automatically mean safe. Keep honey and juice off the menu before the first birthday, and continue breast milk or formula. Today's small win is one simple container game and a check that every toy is age-appropriate, intact, and too large to choke on.

These are general ideas, not a substitute for your child's care plan. If feeding, growth, or development worries you, ask your clinician. Sources are included with this episode. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.subtitle: 10 months

episodes.title: Month 11
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month eleven: Prepare for the next chapter. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

The first birthday is coming, but independent walking is not a birthday entrance requirement. The CDC's one-year checklist includes pulling up to stand and walking while holding furniture. Offer a safe place to practice and stay close. Do not use a baby walker; safe floor exploration is a better choice.

This is a good month to plan the next checkup. Write down questions about development, meals, and the transition from formula after twelve months. The CDC says plain, unsweetened, pasteurized whole cow's milk can replace formula at that stage; discuss alternatives or individual needs with the clinician. Breastfeeding can continue if parent and child want it. There is no deadline to stop because a candle appears.

Keep food preparation safe and the sleep space appropriate. Practice a cup with help during a calm meal, and expect spills. Today's task is planning, not rushing: a question list for the clinician and a safe bit of furniture for supported practice. Your baby's pace deserves attention, not a countdown.

These are general ideas, not a substitute for your child's care plan. If feeding, growth, or development worries you, ask your clinician. Sources are included with this episode. See you in the next chapter.

episodes.subtitle: 11 months

episodes.title: Month 12: One Year!
episodes.transcript:
Welcome to Little Steps. Month twelve: A year of little steps. This is a listen-ahead guide, not a prediction about any particular baby.

Welcome to the first-birthday chapter. Whether you are listening ahead or arriving at this stage, take a breath. There is no single picture of a one-year-old. The CDC's reference points include waving goodbye, using a special name for a parent, pulling to stand, cruising along furniture, and picking up small bits of food between thumb and finger.

Look at the whole picture and bring questions to the clinician. If a skill has been lost or something concerns you, ask for developmental screening rather than waiting. Celebrate attempts without turning the checklist into a score.

Food and drink move into a new stage. After twelve months, many children can transition from formula to plain pasteurized whole milk, with the clinician helping tailor the plan. Breastfeeding may continue. Keep offering varied, safely prepared foods, help with a cup, and skip sugary drinks; juice is unnecessary. Use positive words and gentle redirection as curiosity grows. Today's celebration can be simple: share a book, a song, or a game together. The next chapter still starts with small, responsive moments.

These are general ideas, not a substitute for your child's care plan. If feeding, growth, or development worries you, ask your clinician. Sources are included with this episode. See you in the next chapter.
